vectors.enisa_quote: This may grant adversaries access to processes, information or even facilites
vectors.reason: ENISA names no origin; the taken-over actor is inferred to be mission ground staff (operator, administrator) because the stolen identity opens 'processes, information or even facilites'.
'Lifecycle actors' includes partners and vendors; ENISA does not say which actor, so a partner or vendor identity used to ride an already trusted connection is the inferred path.
Lifecycle actors also work in integration and test; ENISA's 'facilites' is inferred to include the ATLO site a posed integrator or test engineer can enter. The text names no site.

rows.reason: Blinding or falsifying ground telemetry is not part of taking over an identity; ENISA stops at posing as the actor and the access that follows.

rows.sparta_quote: The adversary presents themselves as an authorized origin so activity appears legitimate
rows.reason: Posing as the taken-over lifecycle actor is the masquerade SPARTA describes, including use of insider-derived credentials or roles.
rows.ground_side_reason: SPARTA describes this technique against the spacecraft or its C2 systems; this threat applies it to the ground IT identity or account that the credential opens (the ENISA affected assets are ground IT systems), so it needs an attacker on the ground side with an accepted entry, not the satellite bus.

rows.reason: Subverting protections in safe-mode is an on-board timing trick; the text describes no step on the spacecraft.

rows.enisa_quote: which would allow adversaries to pose as those actors
rows.sparta_quote: Threat actors may leverage valid credentials to conduct unauthorized actions
rows.reason: The stolen items let the adversary use the victim's valid credentials, which is what this technique does.
rows.ground_side_reason: SPARTA describes this technique against the spacecraft or its C2 systems; this threat applies it to the ground IT identity or account that the credential opens (the ENISA affected assets are ground IT systems), so it needs an attacker on the ground side with an accepted entry, not the satellite bus.

rows.reason: Replaying captured telecommand packets needs no stolen human identity and ENISA describes no replay.

Exploiting on-board design flaws is not described; the impersonated actor is already accepted, so no flaw is needed.
Misusing hardware commands is an on-board step the text never mentions.
Exploiting relaxed checks in safe-mode is not described; a posed identity does not depend on relaxed checks.
Forging time tags, sensor or navigation inputs is signal spoofing; ENISA's take-over is of a person's identity through personal items.
Replaying commands to provoke repeat downlinks is not described; ENISA names no replay.
Tapping the uplink to collect frames is interception of communication, not an identity take-over.
